sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Gin is the most frequently mentioned Go web framework in job descriptions and the first framework most Go backend developers encounter. Its httprouter-based routing is significantly faster than stdlib ServeMux for large route tables, and its built-in binding, validation, and middleware model reduce boilerplate. Understanding Gin deeply — not just its happy path but its sharp edges — is expected in most Go backend interviews. It also serves as a reference point when interviewers ask you to compare frameworks.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: `gin.Engine` wraps httprouter to provide radix-tree-based routing with named parameters and wildcards. `gin.Context` is an extended request/response context created per request — it holds the http.ResponseWriter and *http.Request plus Gin-specific helpers for binding, rendering, and aborting. Middleware in Gin is a `gin.HandlerFunc` — a function `func(*gin.Context)` — and the handler chain is an ordered slice of these functions; `c.Next()` passes control to the next handler in the chain, and `c.Abort()` stops the chain.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Routing and route groups**: `r.GET`, `r.POST`, etc.; `r.Group("/api/v1")` for shared prefix and middleware; named params `/:id`, wildcards `/*path`.
- **gin.Context methods**: `c.Param`, `c.Query`, `c.PostForm`, `c.JSON`, `c.String`, `c.Status`, `c.Header`, `c.Set`/`c.Get` for per-request values.
- **Middleware with abort**: `c.Next()` invokes the next handler; `c.Abort()` stops the chain; `c.AbortWithStatus(401)` stops and writes a status.
- **ShouldBindJSON / ShouldBindQuery**: decodes request data into a struct using struct tags; returns an error you handle; use `binding:"required"` tags with go-playground/validator.
- **MustBind vs ShouldBind**: `MustBind` calls `c.AbortWithStatus(400)` on binding failure — gives you less control; prefer `ShouldBind` and handle errors explicitly.
- **Testing with httptest**: create `gin.New()` engine, register routes, use `httptest.NewRecorder()` and `http.NewRequest` to test handlers without starting a server.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **gin.Context is not goroutine-safe**: the Context object is reused per request lifecycle; if you pass `c` to a spawned goroutine, the goroutine may access it after the request has been handled and the context recycled — always copy what you need or call `c.Copy()`.
- **c.Abort() vs return**: calling `c.Abort()` prevents subsequent handlers from running but does NOT stop the current handler — you still need `return` after Abort in most cases.
- **MustBind calls AbortWithStatus**: this is a footgun in middleware because it writes the status header before your error handler can customize the response.
- **gin.Default() vs gin.New()**: Default includes Logger and Recovery middleware; New is bare — use New in tests and when you want explicit middleware control.
- **Route parameter vs query param**: `:id` is a path parameter required in the URL; `?id=` is a query parameter optional in the URL — easy to confuse when defining routes.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "I reach for Gin when I need route groups with shared middleware, built-in JSON binding with validation tags, and a familiar handler chain model. I always use gin.New() rather than gin.Default() so I have explicit control over which middleware runs, then add Logger and Recovery explicitly. For request binding I prefer ShouldBindJSON over MustBind because I want to write a consistent error response rather than let Gin automatically write a 400. One thing I always watch for is passing gin.Context to goroutines — since Gin reuses the context object after the request completes, you can read garbage data if the goroutine outlives the request; the fix is to call c.Copy() before spawning the goroutine."
